triage.name: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
triage.reason: Nocturnal hand paresthesias with a positive Tinel/Phalen exam and confirmatory nerve study; classic outpatient musculoskeletal-neurology case.

demographics: Women are about three times more likely than men to be affected
Most common in middle-aged and older adults
Often occurs in the dominant hand first, but frequently becomes bilateral
More common in people whose work or hobbies involve repetitive hand and wrist use

risk_factors.text: Repetitive hand or wrist activity (assembly line, carpentry, vibrating tools, knitting, gardening, racquet sports)
Family history of carpal tunnel syndrome in a first-degree relative

comorbidities: Ganglion cyst or other space-occupying lesion in the wrist
family_history: Carpal tunnel syndrome in a parent or sibling
social_history: Occupations or hobbies with repetitive hand/wrist motion

chief_complaints.text: My fingers go numb and tingle at night
I wake up with a pins-and-needles feeling in my hand
My hand feels weak when I try to grip

hpi.onset: Gradual, often over weeks to months; may begin after a period of increased hand use or during pregnancy
hpi.duration: Usually present for weeks to months before the patient seeks care
hpi.progression: Symptoms typically start intermittently at night, then become more frequent and may occur during the day with activities; without treatment, numbness can become constant and weakness may develop
hpi.location: Palmar side of the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger; spares the little finger
hpi.radiation: May radiate proximally into the forearm or even the shoulder, but not into the neck
hpi.quality: Numbness, tingling, pins-and-needles, burning; sometimes a dull ache
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; night symptoms can be severe enough to wake the patient
hpi.timing: Classically worse at night, especially when sleeping with wrists bent; may also occur with sustained hand positions (driving, holding a phone, reading)
relieving: Wearing a wrist splint at night

associated_symptoms.text: Shaking the hand to relieve symptoms (flick sign)
Subjective swelling of the fingers without visible edema
Dropping objects or difficulty with fine motor tasks (buttoning, holding a cup)
Dry or shiny skin on the thumb/index/middle fingers

pertinent_negatives: Constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats)
Recent trauma or injury to the hand/wrist
Weakness or numbness in the feet
Involvement of both hands simultaneously from the start (though bilateral is common over time)

negatives: Deformity of the hand or wrist
argues_against: Inflammatory arthritis (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis) as the primary cause

negatives: Radicular symptoms in the lower extremities

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms often begin in the second or third trimester and are frequently bilateral; they typically resolve after delivery.
Symptoms may be attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and the distribution may be less clear; carpal tunnel syndrome is more common and can be more severe.
May present with more constant numbness and thenar muscle wasting rather than intermittent tingling; pain may be less prominent.
Higher risk and often more severe symptoms; may be bilateral and less responsive to conservative treatment.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; hand exam findings are subtle
general.moderate: Comfortable at rest; winces or shakes the hand when symptoms are provoked during testing
general.severe: Frequent shaking or flicking of the hand; may have visible clumsiness handling objects
general.critical: Marked thenar wasting with poor hand function; may be unable to perform fine motor tasks

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick over the palmar surfaces of the thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers, and compare with the little finger
findings.finding: Decreased sensation in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger) with sparing of the little finger

findings.maneuver: Tap lightly over the carpal tunnel at the volar wrist crease
findings.finding: Tingling or electric shock-like sensation radiating into the median-innervated fingers

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to hold both wrists in full flexion (or press the dorsal surfaces of the hands together) for up to 60 seconds
findings.finding: Numbness or tingling in the median nerve distribution within 60 seconds

findings.maneuver: Inspect the thenar eminence and compare both hands
findings.finding: Flattening or atrophy of the thenar muscles

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to abduct the thumb against resistance (or oppose the thumb to the little finger against resistance)
Ask the patient what they do when symptoms wake them at night
findings.finding: Reports shaking or flicking the hand to relieve symptoms

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to describe when symptoms occur and whether they wake them from sleep
findings.finding: Symptoms worse at night or waking the patient from sleep

findings.maneuver: Test sensation over the little finger and ulnar border of the hand
findings.finding: Normal sensation in the little finger (ulnar nerve distribution)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical spine, assess range of motion, and perform Spurling maneuver
findings.finding: No cervical tenderness, full range of motion, and no reproduction of arm symptoms with neck extension/rotation

findings.maneuver: Test sensation over the ulnar border of the hand and check finger abduction strength
findings.finding: Normal ulnar sensation and intrinsic hand strength

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulses and check capillary refill
findings.finding: Radial pulses 2+ and brisk capillary refill

findings.maneuver: Inspect the wrist and hand for swelling, deformity, or masses
findings.finding: No visible swelling, deformity, or ganglion cyst

labs.caveat: Hypothyroidism is a treatable contributor; a normal TSH does not exclude carpal tunnel syndrome.
Identifies prediabetes or diabetes, which is common in patients with carpal tunnel syndrome and affects management.
Fasting glucose; a random value is less useful than A1c for screening.
Only if inflammatory arthritis is suspected; usually normal in idiopathic carpal tunnel syndrome.
Nonspecific; consider only when inflammatory arthritis is a concern.

findings.text: Old distal radius or carpal fracture with deformity
Degenerative or inflammatory arthritis of the wrist

imaging.preferred_when: When nerve conduction studies are unavailable, not tolerated, or when a structural cause is suspected

findings.text: Enlarged median nerve cross-sectional area at the carpal tunnel inlet
Flattening of the median nerve within the tunnel
Increased nerve echogenicity with loss of fascicular detail
Ganglion cyst or other space-occupying lesion compressing the nerve
Tenosynovial thickening or fluid around the flexor tendons
Median nerve enlargement and increased T2 signal within the carpal tunnel
Volar bowing of the flexor retinaculum
Ganglion cyst, lipoma, or other mass compressing the median nerve

initial.why: Hypothyroidism is a common, treatable contributor to carpal tunnel symptoms
Screens for diabetes and prediabetes, which are common in this population
Looks for prior fracture, deformity, or arthritis
initial.only_if: history of wrist trauma, deformity, or focal bony tenderness

confirmatory.why: Confirms median nerve compression at the wrist, grades severity, and excludes other neuropathies or radiculopathy
confirmatory.only_if: Confirms median nerve compression at the wrist, grades severity, and excludes other neuropathies or radiculopathy

supporting.why: Alternative or adjunct when nerve conduction studies are unavailable or a structural lesion is suspected
supporting.only_if: nerve conduction studies are not available, not tolerated, or a mass is suspected

supporting.why: Evaluates for a space-occupying lesion or structural cause
supporting.only_if: atypical features, suspected mass, or poor response to treatment
joint pain, swelling, or prolonged morning stiffness
joint pain, swelling, or prolonged morning stiffness

not_indicated.why: No role in the routine evaluation of carpal tunnel syndrome
Not needed unless another metabolic cause is suspected

decision_points: Nerve conduction studies are the standard confirmatory test; order them when the diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms are severe or progressive, or surgery is being considered
Check TSH and A1c because hypothyroidism and diabetes are common and treatable contributors
Image the wrist only when trauma, deformity, focal bony tenderness, or a mass is suspected
Consider cervical radiculopathy or polyneuropathy when symptoms extend beyond the median nerve distribution or are bilateral and symmetric

differential.name: Cervical radiculopathy (C6/C7)
differential.why_considered: Neck and arm paresthesias can mimic hand numbness, and both are common in middle-aged adults
differential.trigger: Neck pain, symptoms radiating from the neck down the arm, or paresthesias beyond the median nerve distribution

history: Neck pain or stiffness
Symptoms radiate from the neck down the arm in a dermatomal pattern
Symptoms worsened by neck extension or rotation
No nocturnal predominance
exam: Positive Spurling maneuver reproducing arm symptoms
Decreased biceps or triceps reflex
Dermatomal sensory loss that may include the little finger or forearm
Normal Tinel and Phalen tests
imaging: MRI of the cervical spine showing nerve root compression
Cervical spine x-ray showing degenerative changes or foraminal narrowing

differential.name: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Diabetes is a common comorbidity and cause of hand numbness and tingling
differential.trigger: Known diabetes with symmetric numbness, or symptoms extending beyond the median nerve distribution

history: Long-standing diabetes
Symmetric stocking-and-glove numbness
Symptoms in the feet as well as the hands
No clear nocturnal predominance or flick sign
exam: Symmetric sensory loss in a stocking-and-glove pattern
Reduced vibration and pinprick sensation in the feet
Reduced ankle reflexes
Tinel and Phalen tests may be negative
labs: Nerve conduction studies showing a symmetric, length-dependent polyneuropathy rather than focal median nerve compression

differential.name: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome)
differential.why_considered: Another common entrapment neuropathy causing hand numbness and weakness

history: Numbness in the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger
Symptoms worse with elbow flexion or leaning on the elbow
exam: Sensory loss in the ulnar distribution including the little finger
Weak finger abduction or a positive Froment sign
Tinel sign at the elbow rather than the wrist
Normal median nerve distribution sensation

differential.name: Raynaud phenomenon
differential.why_considered: Hand tingling and color changes can be mistaken for carpal tunnel syndrome

history: Color changes (white, then blue, then red) with cold exposure or stress
Symptoms triggered by cold rather than by wrist position or sleep
exam: Normal sensation and strength between episodes
Normal Tinel and Phalen tests
Possible digital ulcers or sclerodactyly in secondary causes

differential.name: Osteoarthritis of the wrist or thumb base
differential.why_considered: Wrist and thumb pain with hand dysfunction can overlap with carpal tunnel symptoms

history: Activity-related joint pain rather than nocturnal paresthesias
Stiffness after inactivity that improves with use
exam: Bony enlargement or crepitus at the wrist or thumb base
Pain with thumb motion
Normal sensation and normal Tinel and Phalen tests
imaging: Joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis on wrist or hand x-ray

differential.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
differential.why_considered: Inflammatory arthritis can cause wrist swelling and compress the median nerve, and can also cause hand pain and paresthesias

history: Symmetric small-joint pain and swelling
Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
Constitutional symptoms
exam: Synovitis of the wrists and MCP joints
Joint deformity
Symptoms not confined to the median nerve distribution
labs: Positive rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibody
imaging: Erosions and symmetric joint space narrowing on hand and wrist x-ray

differential.name: Multiple sclerosis
differential.why_considered: Demyelinating disease can cause numbness and paresthesias in the hands

history: Symptoms in multiple areas of the body over time
Visual changes, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or gait difficulty
Symptoms not confined to the median nerve distribution and not nocturnal
exam: Hyperreflexia, spasticity, or a sensory level
Optic neuritis or internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Normal Tinel and Phalen tests
imaging: Brain and spinal cord MRI showing demyelinating lesions

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Hypothyroidism causes soft tissue swelling that can compress the median nerve and is a treatable contributor

history: Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation
Dry skin and hair loss
exam: Diffuse goiter or thyroid enlargement
Delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes
Bradycardia
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4

severity.mild: Intermittent nocturnal numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution, no weakness, normal sensation on exam, symptoms relieved by shaking the hand or a night splint
severity.moderate: More frequent symptoms including daytime paresthesias with activity, mild sensory loss in the median distribution, mild thumb abduction weakness, no thenar wasting
severity.severe: Constant numbness, clear sensory loss, thenar muscle wasting, and significant thumb weakness with difficulty with fine motor tasks; nerve conduction studies show marked compression

red_flags.finding: Rapidly progressive weakness or numbness over days to weeks
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a more aggressive process such as a mass, infection, or inflammatory neuropathy rather than idiopathic carpal tunnel syndrome

red_flags.finding: Symptoms extending beyond the median nerve distribution or involving the lower extremities
red_flags.meaning: Suggests polyneuropathy, radiculopathy, or a central nervous system process rather than isolated median nerve compression

red_flags.finding: Severe pain with focal bony tenderness or deformity after trauma
red_flags.meaning: Suggests fracture, dislocation, or other structural injury requiring urgent imaging

red_flags.finding: Bilateral symptoms with systemic features such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an underlying systemic or inflammatory condition

red_flags.finding: Signs of acute arterial insufficiency (pallor, pulselessness, pain, paresthesias, paralysis)
red_flags.meaning: Requires emergency evaluation for vascular compromise

complications.name: Permanent median nerve sensory loss
clues: Constant numbness rather than intermittent tingling
Symptoms present for months to years without treatment

complications.name: Thenar muscle atrophy and permanent thumb weakness
clues: Visible flattening of the thenar eminence
Difficulty with pinching and fine motor tasks

complications.name: Postoperative scar tenderness or pillar pain
clues: Pain at the base of the palm after carpal tunnel release
Tenderness over the thenar or hypothenar eminence

complications.name: Recurrence after carpal tunnel release
clues: Return of nocturnal paresthesias months to years after surgery
Recurrent median nerve compression on nerve conduction studies

special_populations.differences: Symptoms often begin in the second or third trimester, are frequently bilateral, and usually resolve after delivery; conservative treatment with night splints is preferred.
Carpal tunnel syndrome is more common and can be more severe; symptoms may be attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy, so careful median nerve distribution testing is important.
May present with constant numbness and thenar wasting rather than intermittent tingling; pain may be less prominent and recovery after surgery may be slower.
Higher risk and often more severe symptoms; may be bilateral and less responsive to conservative treatment.

key_questions.question: Which fingers feel numb or tingly?
key_questions.looking_for: Thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger, with the little finger spared

key_questions.question: When do the symptoms happen — do they wake you at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturnal symptoms that wake the patient from sleep, worse with the wrists bent

key_questions.question: What do you do when the symptoms wake you up?
key_questions.looking_for: Shaking or flicking the hand to relieve symptoms (flick sign)

key_questions.question: Is it one hand or both?
key_questions.looking_for: Often starts in the dominant hand but frequently becomes bilateral over time

key_questions.question: How long has this been going on, and is it getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months; progression from intermittent night symptoms to daytime and constant numbness

key_questions.question: Have you noticed weakness, dropping things, or trouble with buttons or holding a cup?
key_questions.looking_for: Grip weakness, clumsiness, difficulty with fine motor tasks suggesting more advanced disease

key_questions.question: Does the numbness or pain spread up your arm or into your neck?
key_questions.looking_for: May radiate into the forearm; neck pain or a radicular pattern points away from carpal tunnel syndrome

key_questions.question: Do your fingers ever look swollen even though they don't seem puffy?
key_questions.looking_for: Subjective finger swelling without visible edema

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, thyroid problems, or rheumatoid arthritis?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes, hypothyroidism, and rheumatoid arthritis are common treatable contributors

key_questions.question: Have you ever injured or broken your wrist?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior wrist sprain or fracture causing deformity or swelling

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy-related fluid shifts can cause symptoms that usually resolve after delivery

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had carpal tunnel syndrome?
key_questions.looking_for: Carpal tunnel syndrome in a parent or sibling

key_questions.question: What kind of work or hobbies do you do with your hands?
key_questions.looking_for: Repetitive hand/wrist activity, assembly line work, carpentry, vibrating tools, knitting, gardening, racquet sports

key_questions.question: Any fever, weight loss, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; systemic features suggest an inflammatory or infectious process rather than idiopathic carpal tunnel syndrome

key_questions.question: Any numbness or weakness in your legs, trouble walking, or trouble with your vision or speech?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a central nervous system process such as multiple sclerosis or stroke

accepted_names: Median nerve entrapment at the wrist
reasoning_points: Numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger) with sparing of the little finger
Nocturnal predominance, often waking the patient from sleep, worse with the wrists flexed
Relief by shaking or flicking the hand (flick sign)
Positive Tinel or Phalen test on exam
Sensory loss in the median distribution and, in more advanced disease, thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction
Symptoms and signs confined to the median nerve, with a normal cervical spine exam and normal ulnar nerve function
Contributing conditions considered, such as diabetes, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, obesity, rheumatoid arthritis, or prior wrist injury
Nerve conduction studies confirm focal median nerve compression at the wrist and grade severity when the diagnosis is uncertain or surgery is considered

easy: Middle-aged woman with classic nocturnal median-distribution numbness and tingling
Symptoms wake her from sleep and she shakes her hand to relieve them
medium: Bilateral symptoms in a pregnant patient in the third trimester
Patient with diabetes whose hand numbness is attributed to peripheral neuropathy
Mild symptoms with normal sensation on exam and no weakness
Symptoms provoked by driving or holding a phone rather than only at night
hard: Older adult with constant numbness and thenar wasting rather than intermittent tingling
Patient with neck pain and paresthesias that extend beyond the median distribution (cervical radiculopathy)
Symptoms in a patient with known hypothyroidism or rheumatoid arthritis, where the underlying condition must also be addressed
Atypical presentation with forearm radiation and no clear nocturnal pattern
